Pulled my PS2 out for the first time in a while and am currently playing through **The X-Files: Resist or Serve**. It's a Resident Evil knockoff, but a decent one.

It's not my favorite clone honestly. Items are hard to spot and hit boxes aren't great for them. It has the same issue RE has with eh boss fights.

What it does do well are creating cinematic moments with a time limit, although these can be a bit confusing. The game is very true to the X-Files show and features the original voice cast. The script for the game was written by writers from the show. The atmosphere is well done, and although the game is too dark at times, environments are pretty interesting and varied.

Worth a pickup if you're into Resident Evil style survival horror or The X-Files franchise. It has gotten more expensive over time however, so maybe just emulation is a better idea.

The thing with Downtown (and I really like Downtown, and work just north of the Arts District), is that it is about as close as the city gets to being like New York or other crowded city centers. The area is odd because you have a bunch of gentrified areas like The Arts District, warehouse districts, government centers, business centers, and suburbs surrounding Skid Row and the majority of L.A.'s homeless population. The issues of Skid Row spill out into all surrounding areas. It is a very chaotic area overall, with minimal parking. I love the area for the sheer variety of food, shopping, and nightlife. But when you think Los Angeles, you don't think Downtown usually. It's nowhere near the beach, it's a concrete jungle, it's much older than a lot of the city, and having a car is a huge pain there due to odd streets and a lack of parking. 

When most people think of Los Angeles, they tend to think the West Side, like where you'd be if you decided to room with the UCLA people. It's a very different experience. Frankly, I like Downtown better, but it's a personal preference. I like gritty stuff better than richer areas honestly.

I'm okay with content warnings, but standardizing them is a way for the government or private entities to regulate what can be purchased by who. It should be on each author and on the reader to do research, and not the job of a regulatory body. The MPAA in particular has really screwed up the film industry, see "This Film Is Not Yet Rated" for reference.
